title: The Birthday Collision
prompt: How many people do you need in a room before it is more likely than not that two of them share a birthday? Assume 365 equally likely days. Most people guess around 180. Show why the real answer is far smaller.
solutionSteps: Count the complement: the probability that all birthdays are distinct.
With n people that is (365/365)(364/365)(363/365)...((365-n+1)/365) — each new person must miss every birthday already taken.
The chance of a shared birthday is 1 minus that product. It crosses one half between n = 22 and n = 23.
At n = 23 the probability is about 0.507. Twenty-three people, not one hundred and eighty.
The intuition gap: you are not comparing yourself to everyone else, you are comparing every pair. Twenty-three people make 253 pairs, and each one is a chance to collide.
